# Summary

This report analyses the spending and background of 2,240 customers of a grocery store, using $t$-tests and a simple regression. It asks three questions: what do customers spend their money on, how does their income compare with the local average, and do customers with children at home spend less on wine?

Key findings:

* **Wine is half of all spending.** Of the average €606 that a customer spent over two years on six product groups, €304 (50%) went on wine, followed by meat (€167, 28%)
* **Customers are richer than the local average.** Their mean yearly household income is €52,247 (95% CI €51,199 to €53,296), about €10,200 above the local average of €42,000. This does not depend on one impossible income of 666,666 in the data
* **Customers with children at home spend much less on wine.** They spent €231 on average, against €487 for customers without children, a difference of €256 (95% CI €224 to €288 less)
* **Most of that gap is explained by income.** Parents have lower incomes (€46,474 against €65,706). When income is held constant, parents' wine spending is only €58 lower (95% CI €33 to €83 lower), about a fifth of the raw gap
* **Small samples usually miss real differences.** People with a PhD earn about €3,200 more than people with a Master's in these data, but random samples of 100 customers fail to detect this about 90% of the time

---

# Reading in the data

The data have one row per customer. The file is `customer_data.csv`, saved in the same folder as this document

```{r read-data}
customers <- read_csv("customer_data.csv")
glimpse(customers)
```

There are 2,240 customers and 20 variables. The variables used in this report are

Variable           | Description
------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
`ID`               | Customer identifier
`Year_Birth`       | Year of birth
`Education`        | Education level (Basic, 2n Cycle, Graduation, Master, PhD)
`Marital_Status`   | Marital status
`Income`           | Yearly household income in euros
`Kidhome`          | Number of young children in the home
`Teenhome`         | Number of teenagers in the home
`Dt_Customer`      | Date the customer enrolled, written day-month-year
`MntWines`         | Amount spent on wine in the last 2 years
`MntFruits`        | Amount spent on fruit in the last 2 years
`MntMeatProducts`  | Amount spent on meat in the last 2 years
`MntFishProducts`  | Amount spent on fish in the last 2 years
`MntSweetProducts` | Amount spent on sweets in the last 2 years
`MntGoldProds`     | Amount spent on gold (premium) products in the last 2 years

---

# Checking the data

Before any analysis, I check for missing values, impossible values, odd categories and repeated rows

## Missing values

```{r missing}
customers %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) %>%
  select(where(~ . > 0))
```

Only `Income` has missing values: 24 customers

## Unusual values

```{r largest-income}
customers %>%
  arrange(desc(Income)) %>%
  select(ID, Education, Income) %>%
  slice_head(n=5)
```

```{r oldest}
customers %>%
  arrange(Year_Birth) %>%
  select(ID, Year_Birth, Income) %>%
  slice_head(n=5)
```

The largest income, 666,666, is four times the next largest (162,397) and looks like a data entry error. Three customers were born in 1893, 1899 and 1900, which would make them over 110 years old when they enrolled. I do not change the original columns. Instead I add a column `Income.checked` that is missing when the income is the 666,666 value, and use it wherever the outlier could matter

```{r income-checked}
customers <- customers %>%
  mutate(Income.checked=if_else(Income > 600000, NA_real_, Income))

customers %>% count(is.na(Income), is.na(Income.checked))
```

## Categories and repeated rows

```{r marital}
customers %>% count(Marital_Status)
```

`Marital_Status` has odd categories: `Absurd` (2 customers), `YOLO` (2) and `Alone` (3). `Alone` may mean the same as `Single`. I do not use marital status in the analysis, so I leave it as it is. `Education` has `2n Cycle` and `Graduation`, which are not self-explanatory

```{r education}
customers %>% count(Education)
```

Are any customers repeated? `distinct()` keeps only the unique rows once the ID is ignored

```{r duplicates}
customers %>%
  select(-ID) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  summarise(unique.rows=n())
```

Only 2,039 of the 2,240 rows are unique when the ID is ignored, so 201 rows repeat another customer in everything but the ID. They could be real customers with the same details, or duplicate entries. I keep them all, and return to this in the limitations

## Enrolment dates

`Dt_Customer` is read as text in day-month-year form, so `dmy()` turns it into a date

```{r dates}
customers <- customers %>%
  mutate(Dt_Customer=dmy(Dt_Customer))

customers %>% summarise(first=min(Dt_Customer), last=max(Dt_Customer))
```

Customers enrolled between July 2012 and June 2014

---

# What do customers spend money on?

The six spending columns give the amount each customer spent on each product group. I reshape them into one column of product groups so that they can be compared

```{r spending-long}
spending <- customers %>%
  pivot_longer(cols=c(MntWines, MntFruits, MntMeatProducts, MntFishProducts, MntSweetProducts, MntGoldProds),
               names_to="product", values_to="amount") %>%
  mutate(product=factor(product,
                        levels=c("MntWines", "MntMeatProducts", "MntGoldProds", "MntFishProducts", "MntSweetProducts", "MntFruits"),
                        labels=c("Wine", "Meat", "Gold products", "Fish", "Sweets", "Fruit")))

(  spending.by.product <- spending %>%
     group_by(product) %>%
     summarise(mean.spend=mean(amount)) %>%
     mutate(percent.of.total=mean.spend/sum(mean.spend)*100)  ) %>%
  kable(digits=1)
```

```{r spending-plot, fig.cap="Average amount spent per customer on each product group over two years."}
ggplot(spending.by.product, aes(x=product, y=mean.spend)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x="Product group", y="Average spending per customer (last 2 years)")
```

The average customer spent €606 across the six groups. Wine accounts for €304 of that (50.2%), then meat with €167 (27.6%). Fruit and sweets are small, at €26 and €27 each (about 4% of the total)

The wine spending is very uneven between customers

```{r wine-histogram, fig.cap="Distribution of wine spending per customer. Each bar is 50 wide."}
ggplot(customers, aes(x=MntWines)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=50) +
  labs(x="Amount spent on wine in the last 2 years", y="Number of customers")
```

Wine spending is strongly right-skewed. Many customers spend little or nothing (13 spent nothing at all) while a few spend over 1,000. This matters for the $t$-tests later, because means describe a skewed variable less well than they describe a symmetric one

---

# Is the average customer income €42,000?

The local area has an average household income of €42,000. If customers were typical of the local area, their mean income would be the same

```{r income-histogram, fig.cap="Distribution of customer household income. Each bar is 5,000 wide."}
ggplot(customers, aes(x=Income)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=5000) +
  labs(x="Yearly household income", y="Number of customers")
```

Income is right-skewed, and the single extreme value of 666,666 sits far from every other customer

**Hypotheses.** The null hypothesis is that the mean yearly household income of customers is €42,000. The alternative hypothesis is that it is different

```{r income-summary}
customers %>%
  summarise(mean=mean(Income, na.rm=TRUE), sd=sd(Income, na.rm=TRUE), n=sum(!is.na(Income)))
```

```{r income-test}
customers %>% pull(Income) %>% t.test(mu=42000)
```

NHST approach: The mean income of customers (€52,247) was significantly different from €42,000, $t(2215)=19.16$, $p<.001$

Estimation approach: The mean income of customers is €52,247 95% CI [€51,199 to €53,296], which is €10,247 higher than the local average (95% CI [€9,199 to €11,296])

The extreme value could affect this, so I repeat the test with the checked income column, which leaves it out

```{r income-test-checked}
customers %>% pull(Income.checked) %>% t.test(mu=42000)
```

Without the 666,666 income the mean is €51,970 and the conclusion is the same, $t(2214)=21.80$, $p<.001$. The result does not depend on that one customer. The test makes the 24 missing incomes drop out automatically

---

# Do customers with children at home spend less on wine?

**Hypotheses.** The null hypothesis is that the mean amount spent on wine is the same for customers with at least one child at home and customers with no children at home. The alternative hypothesis is that the two means differ

A customer has a child at home if `Kidhome` or `Teenhome` is at least 1. I add this as a new column

```{r children}
customers <- customers %>%
  mutate(Children=if_else(Kidhome + Teenhome > 0, "At least one child", "No children"))

customers %>%
  group_by(Children) %>%
  summarise(mean=mean(MntWines), median=median(MntWines), sd=sd(MntWines), n=n()) %>%
  kable(digits=1)
```

```{r children-plot, fig.cap="Wine spending for customers with and without children at home. Each bar is 50 wide."}
ggplot(customers, aes(x=MntWines)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=50) +
  facet_wrap(~Children, ncol=1) +
  labs(x="Amount spent on wine in the last 2 years", y="Number of customers")
```

Customers with children are bunched at very low spending, while customers without children are spread much further to the right. A $t$-test compares the means

```{r children-test}
t.test(MntWines ~ Children, data=customers)
```

NHST approach: Customers with at least one child at home spent significantly less on wine than customers with no children at home, Welch $t(970)=-15.68$, $p<.001$. The $t$ is negative because R compares the "At least one child" group with the "No children" group

Estimation approach: Customers with at least one child spent €231 on average, and customers with no children spent €487. The difference is €256 less for parents 95% CI [€224 to €288 less]

Children can be defined in other ways. Counting only young children (`Kidhome`), without teenagers, gives the same conclusion: parents of young children spent €103 and other customers €451, Welch $t(2112)=-30.49$, $p<.001$

```{r young-children}
customers %>%
  mutate(Young.children=if_else(Kidhome > 0, "Young children", "No young children")) %>%
  group_by(Young.children) %>%
  summarise(mean=mean(MntWines), n=n()) %>%
  kable(digits=1)
```

---

# Is it the children, or the income?

Parents might spend less on wine because they have less money, not because they have children. Let us look at the incomes, leaving out the impossible value

```{r income-by-children}
customers %>%
  group_by(Children) %>%
  summarise(mean.income=mean(Income.checked, na.rm=TRUE), n=sum(!is.na(Income.checked))) %>%
  kable(digits=0)
```

```{r income-wine-plot, fig.cap="Wine spending against household income. Each point is one customer. The checked income column leaves out the 666,666 value."}
ggplot(customers, aes(x=Income.checked, y=MntWines)) +
  geom_point(alpha=0.3) +
  geom_smooth() +
  labs(x="Yearly household income", y="Amount spent on wine in the last 2 years")
```

Parents have much lower incomes (a mean of €46,474 against €65,706), and wine spending rises strongly with income (the correlation is .69 once the impossible income is left out). So the two explanations are tangled together. A regression that includes both children and income separates them

```{r wine-model}
m.wine <- lm(MntWines ~ Children + Income.checked, data=customers)
summary(m.wine)
confint(m.wine)
```

NHST approach: Holding income constant, customers with children at home still spent significantly less on wine, $t(2212)=-4.63$, $p<.001$. Income also had a significant positive effect, $t(2212)=39.15$, $p<.001$

Estimation approach: Holding income constant, parents spent €58 less on wine than customers with no children 95% CI [€33 to €83 less]. Each extra €10,000 of income was associated with €103 more spent on wine

So most of the €256 raw gap is explained by income: once income is held constant, the gap is about a fifth as large. A real difference remains, but it is much smaller than the first comparison suggested. This model assumes that wine spending rises in a straight line with income, which the smoothed line in the figure only roughly follows, so even the remaining gap should be treated with some caution

---

# Do people with a PhD earn more than people with a Master's?

Keep only the two education groups, with a known income

```{r masters-phd}
( masters.phd <- customers %>%
    filter(Education %in% c("Master", "PhD"), !is.na(Income)) )

masters.phd %>%
  group_by(Education) %>%
  summarise(mean=mean(Income), sd=sd(Income), n=n()) %>%
  kable(digits=0)
```

**Hypotheses.** The null hypothesis is that mean income is the same for people with a PhD and people with a Master's. The alternative hypothesis is that it differs

```{r masters-phd-test}
t.test(Income ~ Education, data=masters.phd)
```

NHST approach: People with a PhD earned significantly more than people with a Master's, Welch $t(792)=-2.28$, $p=.023$. The test compares Master's with PhD, so a negative $t$ means the PhD mean is higher

Estimation approach: The mean income was €56,145 for people with a PhD and €52,918 for people with a Master's. People with a PhD earned €3,228 more 95% CI [€454 to €6,001]. The interval is wide: the difference could be anything from small to fairly large

## How often does a small sample miss this difference?

The difference above is only just significant in 846 people. What if we only surveyed 100? I take many random samples from these 846 people, run the same test on each, and count how often the test fails to find that the PhD group earns more. A sample "finds" the difference only when $p<.05$ and the PhD mean is higher. The function `slice_sample()` takes each random sample and `map_dfr()` repeats it 1,000 times. I do not set a seed, so the proportions change a little every time the report is knitted

```{r simulation}
simulate.failure.rate <- function(sample.size, no.samples=1000) {
  many.samples <- map_dfr(1:no.samples, ~ slice_sample(masters.phd, n=sample.size) %>% mutate(sample=.x))

  many.samples %>%
    group_by(sample) %>%
    summarise(t=t.test(Income ~ Education)$statistic,
              p=t.test(Income ~ Education)$p.value) %>%
    summarise(failed=mean(!(p < 0.05 & t < 0))) %>%
    pull(failed)
}

tibble(sample.size=c(50, 100, 200, 400)) %>%
  mutate(proportion.failed=map_dbl(sample.size, simulate.failure.rate)) %>%
  kable(digits=2)
```

In a run of this code, the test failed to find the PhD advantage in about 93% of samples of 50 people, 90% of samples of 100, 82% of samples of 200 and 71% of samples of 400. The difference is real in the full data, but a smaller sample has a larger standard error and so usually misses it. A study of 100 people would nearly always conclude that there is no difference. Not finding a significant difference is not evidence that there is none. Only 846 people are available, so samples cannot get much larger, and a sample of 846 is the whole data set

---

# Limitations

* **Confounding.** Income explains most of the link between children and wine spending, and other things we have not controlled for (age, marital status, education) may explain more. The regression does not show that children cause lower wine spending
* **Observational data.** Having children is not randomly assigned, so no comparison here is an experiment
* **Skewed spending.** Wine spending is strongly right-skewed, and the median for parents (€91.50) is far below their mean (€230.91). With groups of 1,602 and 638 customers the $t$-test is fairly robust, but the mean may not describe a typical customer
* **Data quality.** There are 24 missing incomes, one impossible income, three birth years of 1900 or earlier, unclear marital status categories and 201 repeated rows. If the repeats are duplicates, the sample is effectively smaller than it looks and the standard errors are too small. I did not change the original data
* **Who is in the sample.** These are customers of one store, so the results tell us about this store's customers, not about parents or the local population in general. Customers enrolled at different times between 2012 and 2014, but spending covers the last two years for everyone
* **Definitions.** "Child at home" can be defined in several ways. Young children only, or children and teenagers, give the same conclusion here, but they give very different gaps (€348 against €256)
* **Sampling experiment.** The simulation reuses the same 846 people, so it shows how small samples behave but cannot show how often the PhD advantage would appear in a new population

# Reproducing this report

1. Save `customer_data.csv` next to this `.Rmd`
2. Install the packages with `install.packages(c("tidyverse", "knitr"))`
3. Knit the document in RStudio, or run `rmarkdown::render("Customer-Spending-Analysis-Report.Rmd")`
